analysis.one_liner: Requires health insurers to publish negotiated prices and give personal cost estimates before care.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee vote or floor action before Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have written into law that group health plans and insurers must publish the negotiated rates they pay providers, disclose what they actually pay for drugs net of rebates, and give members a self-service tool that tells them their estimated out-of-pocket cost for a specific item or service from a specific provider before they get care. It builds on price transparency rules the agencies adopted in 2020, adding a statute so the requirements could not simply be undone or weakened by a future administration, and it requires the information be available for free without an account, in plain language, including for people with limited English proficiency or disabilities. It was introduced by a Republican with Democratic cosupport, referred to three committees, and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: Insured workers and families who want to know what a procedure or drug will actually cost them before they get it, employers shopping for plans, and researchers or comparison tools that could use the published rate files.

how_it_helps.text: The bill requires plans to let individuals see, in real time through a free self-service tool, the estimated cost sharing (deductible, copay, coinsurance) they would owe for a specific item or service from a specific provider, including any prior authorization or step-therapy requirements.

Plans would have to publish, in machine-readable files updated at least quarterly, the negotiated in-network rates for every provider, the average amount paid for each drug net of rebates and discounts, and what they allowed for out-of-network care, all accessible free without a user account and comparable across plans.

The requirements would be written into the Internal Revenue Code, the Public Health Service Act, and ERISA, giving the 2020 transparency rule the force of statute, and plans must post an attestation that the published information is complete and accurate.

The bill directs the three relevant departments to make the information accessible in plain language, with translations and assistive services for people with limited English proficiency or disabilities.

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers and employer-sponsored plans bear the cost of building and maintaining the disclosure tools and files, and hospitals, providers, and pharmacy benefit intermediaries whose negotiated rates and net drug payments would become public.

drawbacks.text: Compliance costs fall on insurers and employer plans, which maintain the self-service tools and the machine-readable files; smaller employer plan sponsors could face meaningful administrative burdens.

Disclosure does not by itself lower prices: the machine-readable rate files are large technical datasets that most consumers would not use directly, so the main users would be comparison tools and employers, and savings depend on those intermediaries and on plans and providers actually competing on the newly visible prices.

The bill exempts grandfathered health plans from the rate publication requirement and lets the Secretary exclude certain information categories, so coverage of the disclosure mandate is not universal.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is real and matches what many consumers say they want: knowing your expected out-of-pocket cost before you get care, and seeing what your insurer actually pays. The main costs are administrative, borne by insurers and large employers, and the consumer-facing benefit depends partly on third-party tools making the raw data usable. On balance a fairly modest, targeted bill whose benefits plausibly outweigh its compliance costs, though it is not a price-control measure and would not force prices down on its own.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to three House committees in July 2023, got two subcommittee referrals, and never reached a markup or a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick introduced the bill on July 26, 2023, joined by Rep. Susie Lee of Nevada; two House Democrats cosponsored it.
The House referred it to the Energy and Commerce, Education and the Workforce, and Ways and Means committees, with subcommittee referrals in July 2023 and again in December 2024.

No committee reported the bill and no chamber voted on it; the full action history ends with the December 2024 subcommittee referral, and the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 without the bill advancing.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers, hospitals, and other providers benefit from the bill's death: their negotiated rates and net drug payments stay out of any statutory disclosure mandate, and insurers remain free of the requirement to build the personalized cost-estimate tool into law. Because the 2020 transparency rule remains in effect by regulation, much of the rate disclosure already happens, but the added statutory backing and the personalized cost tool died with the bill.

for.name: Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Health Insurance Price Transparency Act of 2023 in the House.

for.name: Rep. Susie Lee
for.role: Original Democratic cosponsor, House member from Nevada
for.what_they_did: Joined the Republican sponsor in introducing the bill, making it bipartisan from the start.

against.name: House committee chairs (Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, Education and the Workforce)
against.role: Chairs of the three committees of referral
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup or brought the bill to a vote in roughly 17 months after referral; the bill's last action was a subcommittee referral in December 2024.

sides.party_line_note: There were no votes, so no party breakdown exists; sponsorship was bipartisan, a Republican with a Democratic original cosponsor and two Democratic cosponsors, but no committee or floor action ever tested broader support.

industries.note: The bill would force insurers to publish every negotiated provider rate, their net drug payments after rebates, and personalized cost estimates for members. Insurers have argued these disclosures expose competitively sensitive contract terms; the public interest runs the other way, toward shoppers seeing prices before care.

Their negotiated rates with every major plan would become public and comparable, which could push payers to demand lower rates while also making it easier for consumers and employers to comparison-shop.

Plan sponsors would bear compliance costs for the tools and machine-readable files, but employers as purchasers also gain visibility into what their plans pay providers, which strengthens their negotiating position.
